summary: An April 1st joke RFC proposing the Internationalized Deliberately Unreadable Network NOtation (I-DUNNO), a notation said to replace readable IP addresses with something harder to read. It pokes fun at people who read, write and misspell IP addresses by hand. It is not a serious protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: A joke document about writing computer addresses in a silly code nobody can read, on purpose, for April Fools' Day.

questions: is there an april fools rfc about ip addresses
subtitle: An April Fools' scheme to write IP addresses in deliberately confusing Unicode.

tldr.problem: Humans persist in reading, writing, and misspelling IP addresses despite being designed for machines, when they should only use domain names.
tldr.mechanism: This April Fools' RFC proposes the Internationalized Deliberately Unreadable Network NOtation (I-DUNNO), which encodes IP addresses as UTF-8 sequences with varying confusion levels using emoji, combining characters, and characters from multiple scripts.
tldr.outcome: This is a humorous April 1st document published in 2020 that satirizes Unicode complexity and the challenges of internationalization.

today: RFC 8771 is an Experimental RFC published on April 1, 2020, as an April Fools' Day joke. It is not a real notation and was never intended for actual use in networks.

sections.title: The Problem with Human Meddling
sections.content:
RFC 8771 humorously argues that domain names were designed for humans, but IP addresses were designed for machines. The RFC laments that humans persist in reading, writing, misspelling, and memorizing IP addresses despite the existence of the Domain Name System. The authors propose the Internationalized Deliberately Unreadable Network NOtation (I-DUNNO), a Unicode-based notation that discourages human manipulation of IP addresses by rendering them in deliberately confusing form.

The RFC sardonically praises earlier attempts to hamper human use: the vague specification of textual IP representation in RFC 1123, the additional confusion offered by IPv6 in RFC 4291, and notes that these noble efforts were "unfortunately severely compromised" by RFC 5952, which made IPv6 addresses more readable. I-DUNNO seeks to reverse this trend.
sections.plainLanguage: Humans are not supposed to read IP addresses. This joke proposes making them impossibly confusing with weird characters, so people will stop trying.

sections.title: UTF-8 Encoding and Formation
sections.content:
I-DUNNO converts IP address bits into UTF-8 octet sequences of varying lengths (1 to 4 octets), choosing sequence lengths to maximize confusion. The process works left-to-right through the address bits (32 for IPv4, 128 for IPv6), allocating bits to fill the vacant positions in UTF-8 encoding rules. When fewer bits remain than a sequence requires, padding bits are added, with content chosen to maximize confusion.

The RFC defines three levels of confusion: Minimum (at least one multi-octet UTF-8 sequence and one IDNA2008-disallowed character), Satisfactory (minimum plus non-printable characters or multi-script content), and Delightful (satisfactory plus characters from different directionalities, confusables, or emoji).
sections.plainLanguage: The address bits are turned into weird UTF-8 characters. Some characters are emoji, some are from other languages backwards, some do not even print normally.

sections.title: Confusion Levels and Human Discouragement
sections.content:
The RFC earnestly defines metrics for how effective an I-DUNNO notation is at confusing humans. At the Delightful Confusion Level, the notation includes characters from scripts with different directionalities (left-to-right vs. right-to-left), characters marked as confusables (visually similar to other characters), and emoji. The RFC notes that Delightful-level I-DUNNOs "will cause almost all humans to U+1F926" (shrug emoji), except those subscribed to the IDNA standards mailing list.

The authors humorously discuss a hypothetical even higher "BREXIT" level confusion, but confess they have no idea how to implement it. Unallocated code points must be avoided despite their confusion power, to prevent future Unicode assignments from reducing effectiveness.
sections.plainLanguage: Different confusion levels use characters that look alike, emoji, and backwards text. At the top level, almost everyone gives up except people who obsess over international domain names.

sections.title: Conversion Example
sections.content:
The RFC provides an example converting IPv4 address 198.51.100.164 to I-DUNNO. The 32-bit binary representation is split into UTF-8 sequences of 7, 7, 7, and 11 bits, yielding four code points: U+0063 (Latin small letter 'c'), U+000C (form feed), U+006C (Latin small letter 'l'), and U+04A4 (Cyrillic capital ligature). The resulting string contains a mix of Latin letters, control characters, and Cyrillic characters, confusing while respecting UTF-8 encoding rules.

Reverse DNS usage and MAC addresses are explicitly out of scope. The RFC notes that the occasional human-induced omission of the dot character (U+002E) already causes sufficient disorder in reverse DNS.
sections.plainLanguage: An example: the address "198.51.100.164" becomes a strange mix of Latin letters, control characters, and Cyrillic letters.
